method: Protein sequences were shuffled (preserving AA composition, destroying order) and re-encoded through the 6-bit pipeline. The production vocabulary (1,932 words) was matched against both real and shuffled byte streams, stratified by vocabulary word length.

length_stratified.interpretation: 2-byte patterns are largely composition-dependent; most appear in both real and shuffled sequences.
3-byte patterns show 2.1x enrichment in real sequences and 1.5x higher functional coherence.
4-byte patterns are 22x more frequent in real sequences. Only 28% of 4-byte vocabulary words appear at all in shuffled sequences.
5-byte patterns are virtually absent from shuffled sequences (136x ratio). Only 5% of 5-byte vocabulary words appear at all, confirming these patterns depend entirely on real sequence order.

conclusion: Shuffling protein sequences while preserving amino acid composition progressively destroys vocabulary matches as word length increases: 1.08x at 2 bytes, 2.1x at 3 bytes, 22x at 4 bytes, and 136x at 5 bytes. The 2-byte (composition-dependent) words constitute 50.6% of the vocabulary but the longer words that carry the functional signal are almost entirely absent from shuffled sequences. This confirms that the computational vocabulary is a property of real protein sequence order, not an artifact of amino acid composition or the encoding methodology.
